sections.markdown:
## Cash back: where to pay

| Spending | Per year | Card (in order) | Net rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| rent | $36,000.00 | Test Grocery 4% ($18,040.00) → Test Flat 2% ($17,960.00) | 2.50% / 0.50% |
| travel | $7,200.00 | Test Flat 2% | 2% |
| groceries | $6,000.00 | Test Grocery 4% | 4% |
| dining | $4,050.00 | Test Costly | 2.10% |
| recurring | $960.00 | Test Grocery 4% | 4% |
| other | $60.00 | Test Flat 2% | 2% |

- Gross cash back: **$1,589.45** a year (2.93% of card-eligible spend).
- Card fees not rebated: $150.00. Rent service fees: $540.00. Memberships: $150.00.
- **Net: $749.45 a year.**
- Paid by bank transfer: taxes, transfers and other payments cards cannot take.
- Rent rule (count charges, no math): Test Grocery 4% × 6 → Test Flat 2% × 6 per cap year, starting at each card's cap reset.
sections.title: Cash back: where to pay

sections.markdown:
## Bank accounts: hold the minimum or pay the fee

Cash is valued at 2% a year (a default; set `goals.cash_rate`). Holding a minimum costs that rate minus what the account pays.

| Account | Fee/month | Minimum | Keep | Interest | Holding costs | Fee + rebate lost | Break-even | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Test Bank Package | $30.95 | $6,000.00 | $6,500.00 | 0% | $120.00 | $491.40 | 8.19% | hold the minimum |

- Cash held at bank minimums: $6,500.00 (counts toward the emergency fund).
- Minimums are usually the balance at the end of **every** day; one day below means the full monthly fee.
- Money moves in before it moves out: transfer first, then pay the card the same day.

## Tax: rates and moves

- Estimated 2026 income tax on $120,000.00: $27,852.76 (average 23.21%, marginal **43.41%**).
- Capital gains: half is taxable, so a $1,000 gain costs about $217.05.
- Payroll contributions on employment income: CPP/QPP $4,646.45, EI $1,123.07.
- Using all RRSP room ($20,000.00) cuts tax by about **$7,082.21** (35.41% back on each dollar on average: below your 43.41% top rate, because the deduction reaches lower brackets).
- RRSP contributions for 2026 (window Mar 2, 2026 to Mar 1, 2027): **$0.00** (you $0.00, employer $0.00).
- No RRSP contributions found. Add your Sun Life transaction history to the inbox (connectors show sunlife), or set `[room] rrsp_other` for contributions no export shows.
- Limit $20,000.00: **$20,000.00 left**.
- Within the limit: no contributions so far in this window (to Mar 1, 2027).
- Realized capital gains so far in 2026: $1,000.00 → about $217.05 tax.
- Tax-loss harvesting: selling positions at a loss offsets gains; avoid buying the same asset 30 days before or after (superficial loss).

## Cash reserve and where new money goes

- Monthly spending: $1,922.50.
- Emergency fund: **$5,767.50** (3 months). Keep it in cash or a high-interest account.
- Monthly float: $1,922.50 so card payments never bounce.
- Invest anything above **$7,690.00** of total cash.
- Cash now: $40,000.00 → **$32,310.00 can be invested**.

Order for new money:
1. FHSA (room $8,000.00): deductible now, tax-free out for a first home.
2. RRSP (room $20,000.00): deduction at your 43.41% marginal rate.
3. TFSA (room $7,000.00): tax-free growth, withdraw any time.
4. Non-registered: after registered room is full.
- Down-payment money needed within about 2 years stays in cash or GICs, not stocks. The RRSP Home Buyers' Plan needs contributions to sit 90 days before withdrawal.
- The forecast keeps $26,947.50 of that for later months that dip: invest $5,362.50 now.

sections.markdown:
## Long-term investing: core, placement and screen

*Education and arithmetic on your own data, not personal financial advice. This assistant is not a licensed financial advisor. Check facts marked 'estimate' before you act.*

**Core (growth, about 80% stocks):** one diversified, low-fee fund does most of the work.
- XIC: iShares Core S&P/TSX Capped Composite Index ETF, MER 0.06%. Broad Canadian stocks at very low cost. Eligible dividends get the dividend tax credit in a taxable account.
- XUU: iShares Core S&P U.S. Total Market Index ETF, MER 0.07%. Whole US market in CAD. Holds US-listed ETFs, so two layers of withholding issue in RRSP; fine in TFSA.
- VFV: Vanguard S&P 500 Index ETF, MER 0.08%. Cheap S&P 500 in CAD. Holds US shares directly, so 15% US withholding is lost in TFSA/RRSP (recoverable only in non-registered).

**Where each asset goes:**
- US-listed US equity ETFs (VTI, SCHD, VYM) → RRSP: The Canada-US treaty exempts RRSPs from the 15% US dividend withholding. TFSAs and RESPs are not exempt.
- Canadian-listed US equity ETFs (VFV, XUU, VUN) → TFSA: Withholding is lost in TFSA and RRSP alike; the cost is small (about 0.2%/yr). In non-registered you can claim the foreign tax credit.
- Canadian equity (XIC, VDY) → non_registered: Eligible Canadian dividends get the dividend tax credit only in a taxable account. Also fine in a TFSA.
- Bonds and GICs (ZAG, XBB) → RRSP: Interest is taxed at your full marginal rate; shelter it first.
- Highest expected growth (all-equity ETFs) → TFSA: Tax-free growth compounds best on the assets that grow most.
- All-in-one ETFs (XEQT, VEQT, XGRO, VGRO) → any: Simplicity beats small location gains for most people. Hold the same fund everywhere and rebalance by contribution.
- Short-term cash (CASH, ZMMK, HISA) → TFSA: Interest is fully taxable; a TFSA shelters it and keeps it withdrawable.

- Employer stock EMPL: 71.43% of invested cost, above the 10% guideline.
  Selling down over time (RSUs right at vest add no gain, since their cost is the vest value) cuts the risk of losing job and savings at once.

- Market value of your accounts: not recorded yet. Read them in the browser (playbook `read-investment-balances`), then `bin/cashcast api record wealthsimple --set TFSA=…,RRSP=…`.

## Investment moves: ranked, with evidence

**Answer: do move 1.** Move $32,310 above your reserve to a higher-rate safe account you can withdraw in time (first do the steps in move 1). Gain until you need it: $183 to $366 a year. *Not personal advice: you decide.*

*Education and arithmetic on your own data, not personal financial advice. This assistant is not a licensed financial advisor. No stock picks, no market timing: every gain below is a range from long-run planning assumptions, not a forecast. No provider pays for any recommendation. The ranking is fixed rules in code; chat explanations come from an AI model and can be wrong.*

Question any move: say "challenge `<id>`" (skill `invest-challenge`). Override one in profile.toml under `[[invest.overrides]]` with `move`, `reason` and an optional `until` date; the plan respects it.

| # | Move | Long-run average gain a year (range, not next year) | One-time cost | Task |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Keep the $26,947.50 set aside for later months in a safe place, at the best rate (needed in about 10 months) (`cash-drag`) | $183 to $366 a year | — | yes |
| 2 | Do nothing (`do-nothing`) | $0 (baseline) | — | no |

### 1. Keep the $26,947.50 set aside for later months in a safe place, at the best rate (needed in about 10 months) (`cash-drag`)

- **Do:** Move $32,310 above your reserve to a higher-rate safe account you can withdraw in time; if it is for a first home, put up to $8,000 of it in your FHSA (First Home Savings Account), in savings you can withdraw in time inside it
- **Gain vs. doing nothing:** $183 to $366 a year.
- **Why:** You need this money within 10 months, too soon for stocks. A high-interest account, GIC (a deposit with a fixed rate and term) or cash ETF pays about 2.4% versus your 0%. If it is for a first home, up to $8,000 of it can sit in your FHSA in the same safe holdings: the contribution is deductible (about $3,473 less tax once, at your marginal rate (the tax on your next dollar of income)) and a withdrawal for the home is tax-free.
- **Risk:** GICs lock money until maturity; cash ETFs are not CDIC (the federal deposit insurance)-insured.
- **Assumes:** After tax at your marginal rate, earned for about 10 months, not a full year. Safe rates near 2.4% (planning assumption; low end half of the gap).
- **Assumes:** The FHSA tip applies only if this money is for a first home.
- **Strongest objection:** Markets can fall about 42% in a bad year (estimate, `one-year-drop`); money invested now may be needed before it recovers.
- **Evidence:**
  - `short-horizon` (heuristic): Money you need within about 5 years (a down payment, say) stays in safe places: high-interest savings, GICs or cash ETFs. Stocks can take years to recover from a fall. [source](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/savings-investments/investing-basics.html), as of 2026-11-01, review by 2027-04-30.
  - `cash-rate-capture` (heuristic): Low end of the gain from a safe account: assume you capture only half the gap between the best safe rate and your current rate (rates change, money moves late). A rule of thumb used only for the low end of a range. No external source: a judgment call, as of 2026-11-09, review by 2027-04-30.
  - `one-year-drop` (estimate): Global stocks can fall about 40% in one calendar year: the MSCI ACWI lost about 42% (net, USD) in 2008. Money you need within a few years does not belong in stocks. [source](https://www.msci.com/documents/1296102/1636401/ACWI+factsheet/d5d4e6b0-3957-4938-a4aa-dbc956ae93af), as of 2026-11-01, review by 2027-04-30.
  - `pag-short-term` (verified): Long-run planning assumption for cash and short-term deposits: 2.4% a year. [source](https://www.fpcanada.ca/newsdetail/fp-canada--and-the-institute-of-financial-planning-jointly-publish-the-2026-projection-assumption-guidelines-for-financial-planners), as of 2026-04-16, review by 2027-04-30.
  - `fhsa` (verified): A First Home Savings Account gives a first-time home buyer $8,000 of room in the first year, then $8,000 a year; unused room carries forward, but only up to $8,000, so the most you can add in one year is $16,000, up to $40,000 for life. Room starts only once the account is open. Contributions are generally deductible, and a qualifying withdrawal to buy a first home is tax-free when all its conditions are met. [source](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/topics/first-home-savings-account.html), as of 2026-11-09, review by 2027-04-30.
  - `tax-rules` (verified): Canada personal income tax 2026: capital gains inclusion rate and TFSA (Tax-Free Savings Account), RRSP (Registered Retirement Savings Plan) and FHSA limits. [source](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/tax-rates-brackets/current-year.html), as of 2026-10-19, review by 2027-01-31.
  - `investing-data` (verified): Fund fees (MERs) and tickers in knowledge/data/investing.toml. [source](https://www.blackrock.com/ca/investors/en/products/309480/ishares-core-equity-etf-portfolio), as of 2026-10-19, review by 2027-04-30.

### 2. Do nothing (`do-nothing`)

- **Gain vs. doing nothing:** $0 (baseline).
- **Why:** Zero effort, zero trading cost, no new tax. It is the baseline every move must beat.
- **Risk:** Your money keeps today's risks: the $32,310 above your reserve earns -2.1% a year after inflation (-$679); EMPL stays 71.4% of your investments.
- **Strongest objection:** Idle cash and drift compound quietly; doing nothing for years has a real cost.
- **Evidence:**
  - `pag-inflation` (verified): Long-run planning assumption for inflation: 2.1% a year. [source](https://www.fpcanada.ca/newsdetail/fp-canada--and-the-institute-of-financial-planning-jointly-publish-the-2026-projection-assumption-guidelines-for-financial-planners), as of 2026-04-16, review by 2027-04-30.

## Risk moves (no expected gain; they cut the chance of a large loss)

### 1. Sell down EMPL from 71.4% to 10% of your investments (`concentration:EMPL`)

- **Do:** Decide whether to sell about $7,740 of EMPL (to 10% of investments)
- **Gain vs. doing nothing:** about $0 (risk move).
- **Why:** Expected gain about $0: one stock and an index have similar expected returns, but the stock's range is far wider, and your pay depends on the same company. A 50% fall in EMPL would cost you about $4,500 today.
- **Risk:** Selling can miss a rally in the stock. Keeping it can lose savings and job at once.
- **Cost:** Tax on the gain you realize: about $0.
- **Assumes:** EMPL valued at $9,000 (cost base (what you paid, including fees), market value unknown); total investments $12,600.
- **Strongest objection:** Selling employer stock realizes tax now and may miss its upside. Weakest evidence: `single-stock-drop` is a heuristic only.
- **Unknown:** How EMPL will do: nobody knows.
- **Evidence:**
  - `single-stock-risk` (verified): Most single stocks lose to Treasury bills over their life: in US data from 1926 to 2016, about 58% did, and the best 4% of companies made all the net gain. One stock is a much wider bet than an index with the same expected return. [source](https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:eee:jfinec:v:129:y:2018:i:3:p:440-457), as of 2018-06-01, review by 2027-04-30.
  - `single-stock-drop` (heuristic): A planning stress test for one stock: a 50% fall. Single stocks spread far wider than an index; most lose to Treasury bills over their life, so a fall of half is a plausible bad case, not a forecast. [source](https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:eee:jfinec:v:129:y:2018:i:3:p:440-457), as of 2018-06-01, review by 2027-04-30.
  - `concentration-limit` (heuristic): Keep any one stock, your employer's included, to about 10% of investments. Your job already depends on the same company. [source](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/save-and-invest/diversify-your-investments), as of 2026-10-19, review by 2027-04-30.
  - `spiva-canada` (verified): 98.8% of Canadian equity funds trailed their benchmark over 10 years to the end of 2025. Professional stock picking rarely beats the index after fees, so this tool does not pick stocks. [source](https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/spiva/article/spiva-canada-year-end-2025/), as of 2026-03-31, review by 2027-04-30.

## What this plan does not know

- Your stock/bond mix: only 28.6% of your investments have a known asset class, so drift from your 80% target is not checked.
- The kind of EMPL: name each under [invest.classes] in profile.toml (`AAPL = "equity"`; equity, bond, balanced, cash, crypto or gold), so your whole mix is checked.
- Today's Bank of Canada rates: none is fresh, so safe-rate and inflation numbers use the yearly planning assumptions. Run `bin/cashcast knowledge refresh`.
- Debt at 8% a year or more: not recorded, so the debt-first rule is not checked. Set `high_interest_debt` under [invest] in profile.toml (0 when you have none).
- Market prices per holding: some holdings are valued at cost. Add [invest.prices] to profile.toml for fee, tax and loss moves.

Your whole mix: stocks 28.6% · of unknown kind 71.4% of $12,600. Crypto and gold do not count as stocks.
Target mix: 80% stocks, from your risk level (growth, a rule of thumb from `risk-equity-shares`). Agents never move money: each task is yours to do.
